The project's [May 2013 release announcement](https://payments.mifos.org/blog/cosm-ships-mifos-x-platform-1-0/) describes an open-source financial-services platform already used by small microfinance institutions. ## Best fit: BlockTube

I would start with [BlockTube](https://github.com/amitbl/blocktube). It is designed to filter particular YouTube channels and videos, including channel-ID rules, rather than trying to block YouTube at the network level. Its documentation says playlists and autoplay can continue while unwanted content is filtered. A stable channel ID is the most precise starting point for each ARTE channel you want to exclude.

The practical setup is to add the unwanted uploader through BlockTube's channel-blocking menu, then repeat for any other ARTE channels that appear. Its [dated context-menu instructions](https://github.com/amitbl/blocktube/wiki/Context-Menus) explain the channel-blocking action. A reupload by another uploader will require its own channel or title rule; blocking a broadcaster's official channel cannot identify every copy of its documentaries.

The [options source](https://github.com/amitbl/blocktube/blob/master/src/ui/options.html) contains both a control for advancing after a block and a control that limits blocking to suggestions. The official listing dates version 3.0.5 to August 4, 2024 and links its [public repository](https://github.com/Time-Machine-Development/Channel-Blocker-Manifest-v3). The important unresolved point is autoplay: the inspected listing establishes filtering but does not establish that a hidden recommendation cannot still begin playing. I would check that behavior before using it as protection while dozing.

**3. [YouTube's own Autoplay switch](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/6327615?co=GENIE.Platform%3DDesktop&hl=en).** If the main objective is to stop an unwanted next video from waking you, turn this off on the device you use. YouTube's help explains that the setting controls automatic playback of another related video after the current one ends. This is a direct alternative mechanism, although it also stops automatic continuation into desirable documentaries and does not hide ARTE in search or recommendations. Do not assume the cited explanation covers every playlist mode. The live help article is undated, so its date status is unknown.

**4. [Language & Keyword Filter for YouTube](https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/yt-language-and-keyword-filter/).** This Firefox add-on can filter keywords in video titles, channel names and playlist titles, including content loaded as you browse. A rule matching ARTE could catch branded uploads across more than one uploader, but it can also miss unlabelled copies or match unrelated text. Its description does not establish prevention of autoplay, so I rank it below the channel-focused option and the playback switch for this particular problem. The inspected version, 1.0.3.2 dated October 3, 2026, is later evidence; I have not verified what an earlier version could do.

For the channel-specific requirement, BlockTube is the strongest documented fit among these findings. For stopping surprise playback altogether, the built-in autoplay setting is the simpler fallback. None of these findings establishes that all ARTE-produced material can be recognized regardless of uploader, title or browser changes.

For your requirements, I would first try Continue with Ollama, then add Cline if you need an agent to carry changes across files. A local inference backend is the clearest architectural way to remove dependence on a hosted service's message allowance. It still consumes your own computing resources, and the evidence below does not establish GPT-5 or Claude equivalence.

## Ranked shortlist

1. **Continue with Ollama — first editor-based trial.** The official guide shows local model configuration with separate chat, edit, apply and autocomplete roles. That separation lets you reserve a small model for responsive completions and evaluate a more capable model for editing. The guide includes Qwen2.5-Coder model examples. Check the actual model's tool support before relying on agent mode. [Official integration guide](https://docs.continue.dev/guides/ollama-guide)

2. **Cline with Ollama or LM Studio — strongest fit here for agent-style work.** Cline's repository documents VS Code integration, coordinated edits across files, command execution and reviewable changes. Its local-runtime guide explains how to select an Ollama or LM Studio backend. This is a useful candidate for bug fixing and refactoring, but its results still depend on the chosen model. [Cline repository](https://github.com/cline/cline) · [Local-model documentation](https://github.com/cline/cline/blob/main/docs/running-models-locally/overview.mdx)

3. **Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct — a model to evaluate behind the assistant.** Its official model card gives an Apache-2.0 license, local serving examples, Cline-oriented agent support and a native context capacity of 262,144 tokens. It contains 30.5 billion total parameters with 3.3 billion activated: the activated count should not be mistaken for the entire model's memory footprint. Long advertised context also does not guarantee reliable understanding of every file in a large repository. [Official model card](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct)

4. **Tabby — consider it for a self-hosted completion service.** Its VS Code client documents multi-line completion, codebase questions and inline editing against your own Tabby server. This could suit a developer or team that wants one controlled inference service. It adds server administration, and the material inspected did not establish the same autonomous multi-file workflow as Cline. [VS Code client documentation](https://github.com/TabbyML/tabby/blob/main/clients/vscode/README.md) · [Server repository](https://github.com/TabbyML/tabby)

5. **Aider with Ollama — useful if a terminal workflow fits.** Aider's own documentation shows how to work on a project with a local Ollama model, so it is a plausible option in VS Code's integrated terminal. Its context-window guidance matters because a poorly configured backend can omit needed input. This research did not verify a native inline-completion extension. [Official Ollama integration](https://aider.chat/docs/llms/ollama.html)

## Which local model is good enough?

The evidence supports a practical trial, not a blanket guarantee for client projects. Start with an autocomplete-sized model for frequent small suggestions, and separately test Qwen3-Coder for explanation, edits and tool use if your hardware can run it acceptably. I did not establish a reliable head-to-head result for DeepSeek-Coder-V2 or Code Llama within this search, so I would not rank either above these choices on the evidence collected.

Use a small representative set of your own tasks: a reproducible bug, a change that touches several files, and a refactor with existing tests. Compare whether each assistant produces a correct patch, retains the needed project context, follows tool calls reliably, and finishes quickly enough to help. This is a proposed evaluation method; I did not run those experiments or use these tools on your project.

For a large codebase, make sure the assistant can identify the files relevant to the task and that the backend actually receives enough context. A large advertised token limit alone is insufficient evidence of repository-wide reliability.

## Usage limits and evidence limits

Self-hosting removes reliance on a vendor-granted inference allowance for the requests you run locally; hardware capacity and processing time become the constraints. An open-source extension pointed at a hosted API still inherits that API's limits and pricing. None of the primary evidence inspected proves a free, unlimited hosted replacement with frontier-model quality.

These recommendations come from public primary documentation and code-repository pages, not personal deployment experience. The question's cutoff is July 13, 2026, while this search ran on November 21, 2026. ## What I would try first

**Start by evaluating Cline in VS Code with Ollama and a local Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct model, if your machine can run it comfortably.** This is a documented integration route for the multi-file agent work you describe. For inline completion, evaluate a separate local completion setup rather than assuming that every coding agent supplies Copilot-style suggestions.

The key distinction is between the extension and the inference backend. An open-source extension connected to a hosted model can still encounter that provider's limits. Running the model on your own machine removes dependence on hosted inference quotas; that is an architectural conclusion from the documented local configurations, not a promise of unlimited speed or capacity. Hardware, memory and model quality then become the constraints. [Cline local-model setup](https://docs.cline.bot/running-models-locally/overview)

I have not run these tools on your project, so this is a source-grounded shortlist, not a claim of firsthand client-project experience. I also did not establish that any free local setup matches GPT-5 or Claude across the tasks you listed.

## Ranked shortlist

| Rank | Candidate | Why it is relevant | Main qualification |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | [Cline](https://github.com/cline/cline) with a local backend | Its official project documents VS Code integration, coordinated edits across files, terminal work and local providers. | Local task quality and latency need testing; the inspected sources do not establish inline autocomplete. |
| 2 | [Continue](https://github.com/continuedev/continue) with Ollama | Its public source separates local chat/edit/apply, autocomplete and embedding roles. | The current repository explicitly says it is no longer actively maintained and describes a final 2.0.0 release. |
| 3 | [Kilo Code](https://github.com/Kilo-Org/kilocode) with local Ollama | Another open-source VS Code agent with documented local configuration. | Check all model routes and the exact extension version; fully local autocomplete remains unresolved in the inspected material. |
| 4 | [Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct) | A concrete local model to evaluate behind an extension. | It is a model component, not a complete VS Code assistant. |

### 1. Cline: the first multi-file agent I would evaluate

Cline's public repository identifies an Apache-2.0 license, a VS Code extension, project-wide edits and reviewable changes. Its provider list includes Ollama and LM Studio. Those are relevant capabilities for code generation, bug fixing and refactoring across files; they do not prove that a particular local model will perform those tasks reliably. [Cline project](https://github.com/cline/cline)

The local setup is straightforward in principle: run the local server, choose Ollama in Cline's settings, use the documented local address, and select your model. The current guide also describes a compact-prompt option. [Cline local-model instructions](https://docs.cline.bot/running-models-locally/overview)

### 2. Continue: useful for local completion, with a maintenance caveat

Continue remains relevant because the inspected public implementation assigns Ollama to separate chat/edit/apply, autocomplete and embedding roles. That separation lets you evaluate a smaller completion model independently from the model handling interactive edits. [Continue local configuration source](https://github.com/continuedev/continue/blob/main/core/config/onboarding.ts)

Its official autocomplete search extract recommends a small Qwen2.5-Coder model for local completion; I did not independently open the full autocomplete guide in this review. Treat that as a starting configuration to verify, not proof of end-to-end agent performance. [Official autocomplete guide](https://github.com/continuedev/continue/blob/main/docs/customize/deep-dives/autocomplete.mdx)

The current maintenance statement matters for a client workflow. It is not an automatic exclusion—you did not require active maintenance—but I would verify compatibility with your installed VS Code/runtime before committing to it. [Continue repository and final-release statement](https://github.com/continuedev/continue)

### 3. Kilo Code: another local agent, but inspect every route

Kilo's repository identifies an MIT license and a VS Code extension. Its local provider documentation gives an Ollama setup distinct from Ollama Cloud. [Kilo project](https://github.com/Kilo-Org/kilocode) · [Local Ollama setup](https://kilo.ai/docs/ai-providers/ollama)

There is a consequential configuration detail: the current routing guide allows a small-model fallback to Kilo Gateway. It recommends explicitly setting local models and explains how logging out prevents Gateway inference. For autocomplete, that same guide directs users to Mistral BYOK or to disable the feature. A separate feature-page search result advertises local autocomplete, so I would not promise an entirely local completion-plus-agent setup without matching the installed version to its configuration documentation. The narrower local-agent route is documented. [Model routing guide](https://kilo.ai/docs/code-with-ai/agents/model-selection)

## Which local models are worth evaluating?

**Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct is my first trial choice from the models investigated here.** The official card names Cline support, describes its tool-call format, marks Apache-2.0 licensing and lists local runtimes. It has 30.5 billion total parameters with 3.3 billion active per token; the smaller active count does not make its storage equivalent to a 3-billion-parameter model. Its native context is 262,144 tokens, but the card explicitly suggests reducing context when memory runs out. [Official model card](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct)

Kilo's local guide recommends the 30B variant while warning about tool-call failures. It suggests 24 GB or more of GPU memory, or 32 GB or more of unified memory, for the discussed local models at useful speed. Those are guide recommendations, not a guarantee for every quantization, runtime or context setting. [Kilo's local-model guidance](https://kilo.ai/docs/ai-providers/ollama)

For the other models you named:

- **DeepSeek-Coder-V2:** the official README search extract distinguishes the 16B Lite models from the much larger 236B models, and distinguishes its MIT code license from the separate model license. It states that commercial use is supported. I have not established the exact local agent integration or comparative results for your workload. [Official README](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-Coder-V2/blob/main/README.md)
- **Code Llama:** the official README search extract documents separate completion, infilling and instruction variants, with license terms for the weights. That makes the exact variant important. I found insufficient evidence in this review to prefer it as a complete agent backend over the documented Qwen route. [Official README](https://github.com/meta-llama/codellama/blob/main/README.md?plain=1)

These are not rejected for an invented requirement. They are simply less well verified here. Neither a download count nor a vendor benchmark would establish that a model is good enough for your particular client project.

## Avoiding interruptions without bypassing terms

A licensed, locally hosted model used through a supported extension configuration is the concrete route I would test. Keep every inference role local, including auxiliary model calls where the extension has them. That avoids needing a workaround for someone else's quota. Free hosted models can still be useful, but Kilo's own guide says promotional availability changes; I would not build an uninterrupted workflow on an unverified promise of free unlimited hosting. [Model routing and free-model caveats](https://kilo.ai/docs/code-with-ai/agents/model-selection)

For the large-codebase question, evaluate how the assistant finds and edits the relevant files. A long advertised context window alone does not demonstrate repository understanding or correctness. My proposed trial would use a small set of actual tasks: explain one unfamiliar module, fix a failing test, make one change spanning several files, and perform a constrained refactor. Compare correctness, unwanted changes, tool-call failures and elapsed time against your existing workflow. That is an evaluation plan, not a test I have already performed.

**My practical choice is therefore Cline plus a local Qwen trial, with Continue considered separately for local completion if its maintenance status is acceptable.** Kilo is a reasonable additional agent candidate once its version-specific routing is checked. Without your hardware and project measurements, recommending any of them as a proven frontier-model replacement would overstate the evidence.

Research timing: these sources were checked on 2026-11-21. Most are undated live pages, so I have not assumed that their present maintenance statements or configuration details were already true on the question's 2026-07-13 date.

## Recommended direction

For this rebuild, I would start with **Laravel**, retain the existing business rules behind a small application-service layer, and use **Blade/Breeze plus Livewire** for account screens and ordinary interactions. This recommendation is an inference from your existing PHP experience and the need to finish quickly. It does not assume that ten-year-old PHP or Perl code can be dropped into a modern framework unchanged.

Keep the drag-and-drop behavior in the browser and persist completed moves to the server. If the component editor needs substantial local state, previews, undo, or many interactions before saving, **Vue through Inertia** is the alternative I would investigate before committing to Livewire throughout.

The following candidates are ranked by practical usefulness to the described site. Some are the application framework and others cover a specific feature; they are not eight competing complete solutions.

1. **Laravel 9, with Breeze as a starting point** — [framework release notes](https://laravel.com/docs/9.x/releases) and [starter kits](https://laravel.com/docs/9.x/starter-kits). Laravel provides a PHP application structure for the database-backed account and component/group workflows, while Breeze scaffolds account authentication. That keeps the main implementation language familiar and gives you a concrete starting point. The official release table dates Laravel 9 to February 8, 2022 and states that it requires PHP 8.0 or later. Adapt and test the old business logic behind the new controllers; this is not an automatic migration of old PHP, Perl, database schemas, or user passwords. The present starter-kit documentation is not independently dated to the question's cutoff.

2. **Livewire 2** — [official quickstart](https://laravel-livewire.com/docs/2.x/quickstart/). Livewire components combine PHP classes and Blade views and update a page after actions without a full reload, making it a useful option for selection controls, forms, account settings, and group-management screens. This can limit the amount of unfamiliar frontend architecture you must learn. I would still let a browser-side drag library handle the motion itself, and send completed edits to the server; a highly stateful editor needs a prototype before assuming Livewire is the best fit. The opened versioned documentation is undated, so its cutoff status remains unknown.

3. **SortableJS** — [public source and README](https://github.com/SortableJS/Sortable/blob/master/README.md). Its cross-list dragging, grouping options, drag events, and item-ID serialization are directly relevant to moving selected components between saved groups. You would map a completed drop to an authenticated server operation containing the component ID, group ID, and order. SortableJS supplies the browser interaction; it does not supply user accounts, database persistence, or business-rule validation. Thousands of saved items also do not imply that every item should be rendered simultaneously: search, paging, or a limited working set is an application design decision. The opened source is the current master branch, so I have not backdated its exact capabilities.

4. **Laravel Excel 3.1** — [export quickstart](https://docs.laravel-excel.com/3.1/exports/). Its documented export object and controller download flow can produce the user's Excel file from application data, avoiding a custom spreadsheet writer. Define explicit export columns and scope the query to the requesting user's permitted records and groups. The simple example loads a collection; large exports need separate memory and execution-time assessment. This is an export package rather than the application framework, and the opened 3.1 documentation has no verified publication date.

5. **Inertia.js with Vue and Laravel** — [Laravel's documented Inertia integration](https://laravel.com/docs/9.x/starter-kits) and [Inertia routing reference](https://v1.inertiajs.com/routing). Laravel documents React/Vue pages connected through Inertia while retaining server-side routing and controllers. This is a plausible alternative when the drag-and-drop editor deserves richer browser-side state but you still want to keep PHP on the server. It introduces a modern JavaScript component model and build workflow, which adds learning work. I would select this approach or the simpler Blade/Livewire direction according to a prototype of the hardest editor interaction. The Inertia page opened without readable body text, so the functional claim is verified through Laravel's primary documentation; exact historical availability of the inspected integration documentation is unverified.

6. **Chart.js** — [official documentation](https://www.chartjs.org/docs/latest/). Its browser chart rendering can display aggregated component-use counts returned by the backend, which covers the statistical graphs in the requirements. Compute the business meaning of usage and the aggregate counts on the server; the chart library does not provide those rules. Its canvas rendering also means chart styling and accessibility require deliberate implementation. The usable documentation page is marked last updated August 7, 2023, after the January 10, 2023 cutoff; I retain it as later evidence, not as proof of the exact feature set available at the question date. Two attempts to inspect a 3.9.1 source failed.

7. **Laravel Cashier for Stripe** — [Laravel 9 billing documentation](https://laravel.com/docs/9.x/billing). Cashier provides documented subscription and payment workflows that could cover the prepaid service if Stripe fits the existing payment arrangement. The document also lists single-charge and checkout paths, so the payment model should be chosen explicitly rather than assuming that “prepaid” means a recurring subscription. A stored-credit balance or a custom entitlement ledger remains your application logic, and changing payment providers may outweigh the package's benefits. The live versioned documentation was opened, but its publication date was not established.

8. **Django 4.1** — [framework overview](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.1/intro/overview/) and [dated release announcement](https://www.djangoproject.com/weblog/2022/aug/03/django-41-released/). Django's model, database, routing, and administrative-interface facilities make it a credible alternative for a database-oriented application. The official release announcement establishes availability on August 3, 2022. For your specific deadline, I rank it below retaining PHP because Python would require translating or separately exposing existing PHP/Perl business logic and learning a different stack. Its administration interface also does not replace your custom customer-facing drag-and-drop editor.

## What I would build first

Prototype one complete workflow: sign in, search the component catalogue, select a component, drag it into a group, reload and verify persistence, then export that user's data. Use that prototype to choose between Livewire and Inertia before rebuilding every screen. Preserve the existing business decisions in explicit functions or services, with representative old inputs and outputs available to check the migration.

A component, a user's saved selection, a group, and a membership/order record are distinct concepts; modeling them separately is my suggested starting design, not a claim about your existing schema. Keep the catalogue searchable and save changes by stable IDs. Add graphs and billing after that core workflow works.

This research identifies useful building blocks, not a tested implementation or a delivery-time guarantee. I found no evidence establishing that any candidate has already been deployed successfully for this particular site.

# On-device alternatives to Wispr Flow

I would start with **Handy** if the operating system is still undecided. For a Mac, **VoiceInk** and **Superwhisper in an on-device configuration** are also direct candidates. **FOSS Voquill** is useful if local text cleanup matters, while **Windows Voice Access** and **nerd-dictation** offer different approaches to the same core need.

The ranking below emphasizes turning speech into text in the application being used. No operating system, price ceiling, licensing requirement or polishing requirement was supplied, so those are tradeoffs rather than exclusions. These are documentation-based candidates, not applications I installed or benchmarked.

## Ranked candidates

1. **Handy — a straightforward cross-platform starting point.** Its public project describes a configurable shortcut or push-to-talk workflow that transcribes locally and pastes into the active text field. It supports Windows, macOS and Linux, with Whisper and Parakeet model options. It is free and open source. Allow the required microphone and accessibility permissions and choose a model appropriate for the machine; recognition speed still depends on the hardware. [Primary project](https://github.com/cjpais/Handy).

2. **VoiceInk — a direct Mac option with explicit offline setup instructions.** Download a local speech model and select it in the relevant mode. Its documentation explains that recognition can work without internet and that plain dictation can run with enhancement disabled. The current requirements are macOS 15 or later, with Apple Silicon the better fit for local processing. Check modes that switch automatically by application or website, because they can select different processing settings. [Offline setup](https://tryvoiceink.com/docs/offline-dictation).

3. **Superwhisper — a configurable desktop voice-typing option.** The primary product page describes global-shortcut or push-to-talk capture, text insertion at the cursor, and offline recognition using on-device models. That matches the requested dictation workflow. Select an on-device configuration and verify any optional formatting separately: the opened material does not establish that every feature or mobile workflow is offline. An attempted model-documentation URL could not be opened, so configuration detail remains less thoroughly checked here. [Product description](https://superwhisper.com/speech-to-text-app).

4. **FOSS Voquill — local dictation with optional local cleanup.** The project advertises Windows, Linux and macOS builds, a global recording shortcut, and insertion into the application at the cursor. It also states that recognition and AI cleanup run on the computer, without an account. That makes it relevant if the desired replacement includes tidying rough speech as well as recognizing it. Its hardware performance and installation experience were not tested in this research. [Project site](https://voquill.org/).

5. **Windows Voice Access — the built-in route on Windows 11.** Microsoft documents dictation and PC control without internet once the selected language files have downloaded. It is available on Windows 11 version 22H2 and later and can be enabled under Accessibility settings. The initial download requires a connection, and the available language list must match the intended use. This candidate is specifically the Voice Access feature described by Microsoft. [Microsoft setup guide](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/accessibility/windows/voice-access/set-up-voice-access).

6. **YazSes — an offline daemon particularly suited to Linux.** Its documented pipeline records while a hotkey is held, performs recognition locally with faster-whisper on the CPU, and types the result into the focused application. Linux is its primary platform; macOS and Windows support are marked preview. Default models target English, and its requirements list at least 4 GB RAM. It is a plausible choice when a CPU-based local workflow and configurable voice commands are useful. [Primary project](https://github.com/MSKazemi/yazses).

7. **nerd-dictation — a small, configurable Linux alternative based on Vosk.** This utility recognizes speech locally and can emit simulated keystrokes or standard output. Its begin/end controls can be bound to shortcuts, and Python configuration can transform recognized text. It requires more setup than a packaged dictation app: install the model, recording utility and appropriate input-simulation tool, then bind the controls. It is useful when scriptability matters more than a polished settings interface. [Primary project](https://github.com/ideasman42/nerd-dictation).

## Choosing and validating a configuration

For a first trial, choose the candidate that matches the operating system, download its local speech model, and test dictation into the applications actually used. Disconnect the network after setup and repeat the test, including any mode that switches automatically. If polishing is desired, test that step separately; local speech recognition alone does not establish that an optional rewrite operation stays on the device.

The source pages were checked on 21 November 2026. They are live and undated, so I have **not established that their current features were available by the 22 September 2026 question date**. All seven candidates therefore have unknown date status. A potentially dated YazSes paper appeared in search results, but its page could not be opened, so it was not used to establish timing.

The unauthenticated grep.app code-search attempt was blocked. I continued with **code-through-web** searches, opened public repository documentation, and inspected indexed Vosk implementation code. No native code-search success is claimed.

I would begin with Qwen3.5-4B in Q6_K, then compare Qwen3.5-9B in Q4_K_M if the larger model fits your actual retain workload. These are research leads, not a verified claim that either matches gpt-oss-20b in Hindsight. I found no matched retain evaluation or measured RTX 5060 8 GB configuration in the sources examined.

Ranked candidates

1. Qwen3.5-4B, Q6_K GGUF
Official model: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B
Quantization files: https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF/tree/main

This is my first trial because its Q6_K file is 3.53 GB, leaving appreciably more room for context and runtime allocations than the larger candidates. The official comparison reports IFEval of 89.8 for the 4B model against 88.2 for gpt-oss-20b. That gives a reason to investigate instruction adherence, but it is not evidence of equivalent extraction quality after quantization. Qwen3.5 thinks by default; test its supported non-thinking setting for the retain workload and check what quality changes. Its hybrid attention architecture also makes using a compatible llama.cpp build essential.

2. Qwen3.5-9B, Q4_K_M GGUF
Official model: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B
Quantization files: https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.5-9B-GGUF/tree/main

This is the quality-oriented second trial. The same official comparison gives the 9B model IFEval of 91.5, and its Q4_K_M file is 5.68 GB. A fit is plausible with bounded context, but the file size is not a VRAM measurement. Treat the 9B configuration as conditional until the maximum retain input and output complete without weight, cache, or tensor computation spilling to CPU. Its higher-bit files leave much less room: Q5_K_M is 6.58 GB and Q6_K is 7.46 GB.

3. Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Q6_K or Q8_0 GGUF
Official model: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507
Quantization files: https://huggingface.co/bartowski/Qwen_Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-GGUF

This is a useful compact, direct-response baseline. The official model is explicitly non-thinking, and the quantization table lists Q6_K at 3.31 GB and Q8_0 at 4.28 GB. It could give you more freedom to preserve weight precision while keeping a practical context budget. Its published instruction-following and tool-use results justify testing, but I found no direct retain comparison with gpt-oss-20b.

4. Ministral 3 8B Instruct 2512, Q4_K_M GGUF
Official model: https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Ministral-3-8B-Instruct-2512
Quantization files: https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Ministral-3-8B-Instruct-2512-GGUF/tree/main
Dated release: https://mistral.ai/news/mistral-3/

This offers a different dense-model family with native JSON output and function calling. The listed Q4_K_M language-model file is 5.2 GB. Use the text-only path for retain; the repository distributes vision projection files separately. The official FP8 configuration targets 12 GB VRAM, so the 8 GB proposal depends on further quantization and limited context. The family launch is dated December 2, 2025, before the question cutoff, although the exact currently listed quantization artifact was not independently dated.

5. llama.cpp schema-constrained output and explicit placement
Documentation: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/server/README.md
Public source: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/include/llama.h
Windows/CUDA build guidance: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/build.md

This supporting mechanism may matter as much as the model choice: use the local chat endpoint with the required JSON schema, explicitly request all model layers on the GPU, and set a bounded context rather than inheriting a huge advertised maximum. The current server exposes GPU placement, automatic-fit, context and cache-type controls. Schema constraints can reduce format failures; they cannot ensure that the extracted entities, relationships or facts are correct.

How I would select among them

Start with one concurrent retain job and a modest context such as 4K, increasing it only to the size your actual prompts require. Include the output budget when choosing that limit. Inspect startup placement and memory reporting, then run a worst-case sample while observing dedicated GPU memory. A successful model load alone is insufficient. If memory is tight, reduce context or batch pressure, or move to the smaller model; investigate supported cache quantization as a separately measured tradeoff.

Compare a representative set of your own retain inputs against the existing gpt-oss-20b setup. Score valid schema output, missed facts, invented facts, entity/relationship consistency, latency and peak dedicated VRAM. Keep prompts and evaluation criteria fixed. The preferred choice is the smallest configuration that meets your extraction-quality threshold on those inputs. Ordinary CPU tokenization and request handling do not themselves imply model spill, so define the acceptance check around model weights and inference placement.

Evidence limits

All file sizes above are decimal GB as displayed by the publishers and exclude runtime allocations. Windows display use, context, buffers and concurrency can change fit. No model was downloaded or executed. Most evidence is from live pages whose full publication date was not established; I have not treated those pages as proven available by July 2, 2026. Native unauthenticated grep.app code search was attempted but inaccessible; public code was instead found through web indexing and the actual llama.cpp header was opened.
